claims.text: The starting material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a primary BCC solid solution.
Typical composite solidification of HfNbTaTiZr produces embedded nanoscale precipitates.
The nanoscale precipitates have coefficients of thermal expansion distinct from that of the BCC matrix.
Phase boundaries between the matrix and precipitates act as stress concentrators during cooling.
Differential thermal expansion between the BCC matrix and precipitates generates significant residual stresses during cooling from solidification.
Thermally generated residual stresses modify dislocation dynamics.
Thermally generated residual stresses alter lattice strains and elastic moduli.
Precipitation structures can substantially increase yield strength in refractory multicomponent alloys.
Residual stresses caused by thermal-expansion mismatch enhance dislocation pinning and precipitation hardening in HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch stresses account for the alloy's unusual stress-strain and thermoelastic behavior across a wide temperature range.
Minor alloying additions can be used to harmonize the CTEs of the matrix and precipitates while retaining a suitable comparison with the standard alloy.
The higher-CTE-mismatch standard alloy will have greater yield strength than the minimized-mismatch variant.
The higher-CTE-mismatch standard alloy will exhibit greater aging hardening than the minimized-mismatch variant.
The higher-CTE-mismatch standard alloy will show a more nonlinear or anomalous temperature dependence of elastic modulus.
In situ X-ray diffraction will show higher internal residual stresses in the standard alloy than in the minimized-mismatch variant.

The baseline HfNbTaTiZr alloy has previously reported tensile-creep behavior at 1250 °C, cold-rolling microhardness changes, elastic-modulus variation from 293 to 1100 K, and aging hardening at 600–800 °C.
The proposed mechanism is relevant from room temperature to 1250 °C, including tensile, creep, cold-deformation, and thermoelastic responses.
Compositional ordering or precipitate evolution may also contribute to the observed behavior.
The comparison should use identical post-solidification cooling rates and measure residual stress, stress-strain response, elastic modulus, thermal expansion, and precipitate morphology.

Statistically indistinguishable residual stress, yield strength, hardening, and elastic-modulus evolution in the standard and minimized-mismatch variants would falsify thermal-expansion mismatch as the primary mechanism.
